synopsis: Berm and dump-point events, rather than object collisions, accounted for most deaths in the cited analysis of 54 US surface-mining haul-truck fatalities from January 2005 to June 2021: 21 involved berms, 12 dump points, 13 people or vehicle collisions, and eight other causes [f2989, f3246]. Of the 12 dump-point deaths, six involved reverse-overs and six ground failures; ten involved absent or inadequate berms and seven drivers were unbelted, supporting consideration of edge, geofence, speed and stability controls alongside object detection [f2999, f3000, f3001, f3250]. Normal production deliberately brings machines close to piles, dump edges and other machines, yet a change of intention can turn tip-head proximity into a collision; the 12 August 2019 Snapper Mine fatality involved a light vehicle struck by a reversing dozer whose operator did not know it was there [f11375, f3356, f3116]. Validation must distinguish intended pile approaches from intrusions without suppressing genuinely dangerous berm detections; Volvo CE uses slope memory to avoid braking while reversing down stockpiles, but published surface-machine stockpile nuisance-alarm frequency data were not found [f11521, f11522, f11392, f3360]. Braking itself can worsen marginal ground support at dump edges, and stockpiles, trailers and close loading are identified as critical false-stop scenarios for testing [f6299, f11011, f11119]. Virtual coverage also has gaps: forward-facing route logs miss stockpile backs and other unseen surfaces, OpenDRIVE needs supplementary representations for stockpiles and free terrain, and Scenic fits these settings better than road-oriented languages but is not a standard [f3811, f7158, f6694].
